Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Independent Level (A2+ → B1)

Teacher Copy: Work & Ambition

Week 7 Lesson Plan: Work & Ambition

Concept: A Year at Bay State Fresh. Students follow Maya (a fictional employee) from landing a job to burning out to climbing the ladder, then use the expressions in their own conversations.

Syllabus focus

  • Expressions: climb the ladder, burn out, pull your weight, land a job, be on top of things
  • Grammar: present perfect in context (has been working, has climbed)
  • SLO (B1): use work idioms in role-plays and short written descriptions of work experience, including the present perfect

Recycled

  • Week 1: break the ice, make small talk, hit it off, kill time
  • Week 3: figure out, come up with, give up
  • Week 4: get along, patch things up
  • Final core: be on top of things (and hit it off, figure out, patch things up)
Movement activities (3, short): Opinion Line (Block 1), Office Mingle and Register Corners (Block 2).
Materials: student copy (phones or printed PDF), slides tab, masking tape for the line, 4 corner signs, 16 mingle cards, 6 role-play cards, 8 mission cards, scrap paper for REAL/WEIRD.

Block 1 · Spiral Review

Weeks 1–5 at Work

broke the ice · figured it out · hit it off · patched things up · came up with · killed time · give up · get along

  1. On my first day, a coworker told a funny story about the coffee machine. It really broke the ice.
  2. The printer stopped working, but Sam from IT figured it out in five minutes.
  3. My new manager and I hit it off right away. We both love soccer.
  4. We had an argument about the schedule, but we patched things up the next day.
  5. Our team came up with a great idea for the holiday party.
  6. I was early for my interview, so I killed time in a coffee shop.
  7. The project is hard, but please don't give up. We're almost done!
  8. I get along with everyone on my team. They're really nice.

Block 1 · Engage

Maya's Year in 6 Texts

A Big news: they made me team lead! One year ago I was answering phones. I'm slowly climbing the ladder.
B 60 hours this week. No lunch breaks. I almost fell asleep on the train. I think I'm burning out.
C I GOT IT!!! After five applications, I finally landed a job at Bay State Fresh! I start Monday.
D Talked to my manager. She split the work more fairly and told me to take my breaks. I feel human again!
E New project with Kevin and two others. Kevin keeps missing meetings. Honestly, he's not pulling his weight.
F Week 3 and everything's great. Color-coded calendar, inbox at zero. I'm totally on top of things.

Put them in order. What happened to Maya? Order: C → F → E → B → D → A

Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Do NOT teach the expressions yet. Pairs read and put the texts in order (Part 1 on the student copy) and tell Maya's story in their own words. Ask: Was Maya happy all year? When was the worst moment? Then press R. Next slide: guess the meaning.
Block 1 · Engage

What do you think it means?

  • landed a job = got a job after trying
  • on top of things = organized, in control
  • not pulling his weight = not doing his fair share
  • burning out = very tired and stressed from too much work
  • climbing the ladder = moving up to better jobs, step by step
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Students finish the guess-the-meaning part of Part 1 on the student copy. Elicit guesses before pressing R. Praise good guesses even if not perfect: the goal is noticing.
New Expression 1 of 5

land a job

Maya sent five applications to Bay State Fresh. Five! Last week the phone rang: "You got the job." She landed a job.

Think: What does "landed a job" mean here?

Meaning: to get a job, usually after trying hard (a job that many people want)
Pattern: land + a job / an interview / a role / a contract / your dream job
Example: After six months of searching, my cousin landed a job at a bank.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Situation, then meaning, then notice. Ask the Think question, take 2-3 answers, then press R. Students open card 1 in the Toolkit tab (guess, then open the box). Key point: NOT "land on a job" or "landed to a job." Land takes the object directly: landed a job. Register: Neutral to casual. Fine with friends, coworkers, and your boss. In a formal letter, say "I was offered the position." About 5 minutes per expression including the drill on the next slides.
New Expression 2 of 5

be on top of things

Week 3 at her new job: Maya has a color-coded calendar. She answers every email the same day. She never misses a deadline. She is on top of things.

Think: Is Maya organized or disorganized? What does "on top of things" mean?

Meaning: to be organized and in control of everything you need to do
Pattern: be / stay / keep + on top of things
Example: I use a planner to stay on top of things at work.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Situation, then meaning, then notice. Ask the Think question, take 2-3 answers, then press R. Students open card 2 in the Toolkit tab (guess, then open the box). Key point: NOT "on top of thing" or "on the top of things." Always plural: things. Register: Neutral. Safe everywhere, even in a job interview: "I use a planner to stay on top of things." About 5 minutes per expression including the drill on the next slides.
New Expression 3 of 5

pull your weight

Maya's team has four people. Kevin misses meetings and doesn't answer emails. Maya finishes his part every week. Kevin isn't pulling his weight.

Think: Who is doing their fair share? Who isn't?

Meaning: to do your fair share of the work in a group
Pattern: The possessive matches the person: I pull my weight / she pulls her weight / he isn't pulling his weight / everyone needs to pull their weight
Example: Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight if we want to finish on time.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Situation, then meaning, then notice. Ask the Think question, take 2-3 answers, then press R. Students open card 3 in the Toolkit tab (guess, then open the box). Key point: NOT "pull our weights" (no -s) and NOT "He needs to pull your weight." Match the possessive: his weight. Register: Neutral to casual. Be careful: telling someone "You're not pulling your weight" is direct criticism. With a boss, softer is better: "I feel the work isn't split evenly." About 5 minutes per expression including the drill on the next slides.
New Expression 4 of 5

burn out

Maya is working 60 hours a week. No lunch. No weekends. She feels tired all the time, and she doesn't enjoy her job anymore. She's burning out.

Think: How does Maya feel? What happens when you burn out?

Meaning: to become very tired and stressed (body and mind) because you worked too hard for too long
Pattern: Verb (no object): I'm burning out. / She burned out after two years.
Example: He burned out after two years of night shifts.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Situation, then meaning, then notice. Ask the Think question, take 2-3 answers, then press R. Students open card 4 in the Toolkit tab (guess, then open the box). Key point: NOT "I'm burnout." Burnout is a noun. Say: I'm burned out. / I'm burning out. Register: Neutral. Fine with friends, coworkers, a manager, even a doctor. About 5 minutes per expression including the drill on the next slides.
New Expression 5 of 5

climb the ladder

One year ago, Maya answered phones. Today she is a team lead. In five years she wants to be a manager. She is climbing the ladder.

Think: Is Maya moving up or down in the company?

Meaning: to move up to better jobs in a company or career, step by step
Pattern: climb the (career / corporate) ladder · move up the ladder · a step up the ladder
Example: She climbed the corporate ladder from cashier to store manager.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Situation, then meaning, then notice. Ask the Think question, take 2-3 answers, then press R. Students open card 5 in the Toolkit tab (guess, then open the box). Key point: Don't pronounce the b in climb. And it's not literal: you don't climb on a real ladder. Register: Neutral. Sometimes a little negative: "He only cares about climbing the corporate ladder." About 5 minutes per expression including the drill on the next slides.

Direct or polite?

The Opinion Line

Strongly agreeIn the middleStrongly disagree

Block 2 · Energizer

Real or Weird?

Teams: hold up REAL or WEIRD. If weird, fix it for a bonus point.

  1. She landed a job at the hospital. Real
  2. He landed a coffee this morning. Weird: He got / bought a coffee.
  3. I'm on top of things, so I missed three deadlines. Weird: I'm behind, so I missed three deadlines.
  4. Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight. Real
  5. She pulled her weight out of the gym. Weird: Not an idiom here; it means nothing.
  6. He burned out after two years of night shifts. Real
  7. I'm so burnout today. Weird: I'm so burned out today.
  8. She climbed the corporate ladder from cashier to store manager. Real
  9. I landed my dream job, so I'm burning out with happiness. Weird: Burn out is negative: I'm so happy!
  10. Kevin isn't pulling his weight, so we have extra work. Real
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Teams of 3-4. Each team writes REAL on one side of a paper and WEIRD on the other. Read a sentence, count 3-2-1, teams show. 1 point for correct, +1 for a correct fix. Press R at the end to show all answers.
Block 2 · Grammar

The present perfect at work

Big newsI've landed a job!
ExperienceHave you ever burned out?
Until nowI've been working 60 hours a week since March.
Until nowShe's been on top of things for a year.
Finished timeHe burned out last year. (simple past)
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Teach from the listening: "You've been on top of things since your first day." Concept check: Is she still organized? (Yes.) When did it start? (Her first day.) Then Part 7 in pairs. A2+: focus on items 1, 2, 5. B1: challenge sentences with since/for.
Block 2 · Accuracy

Find and Fix

Each sentence has ONE mistake.

  • Wrong preposition or extra word
  • Wrong word form (noun vs. adjective)
  • Wrong possessive (his / their)
  • since vs. for
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Part 8. Pairs. Elicit the four mistake types before they start. Check together; ask students to explain WHY each fix is right.

Block 2 · Register

Would you say this?

  1. "Kevin is a total slacker." Close friend only. Very casual and rude about Kevin; never to your manager.
  2. "I feel the work on our project isn't split evenly." Manager (best). Polite and professional. Also fine with coworkers.
  3. "I've stayed on top of all my deadlines this year." Job interview or manager. Professional and positive.
  4. "Ugh, this job is burning me out." Close friend or trusted coworker. Casual complaint.
  5. "I landed my first job in the U.S. in 2024." Anywhere. Neutral. Fine in an interview too.
  6. "I'm crushing it at work!" Close friend (text). Very casual slang. Not in an interview.
  7. "My goal is to move up the career ladder in the next five years." Job interview or manager. Professional.
  8. "Honestly, I'm thinking about quiet quitting." Close friend only, and be careful. Never to your manager.
Idioms & Slang · Week 7 · Work & Ambition
Press R after each round or at the end. Students record their choices in Part 10.

Answer Key

Keep this copy private. Students see auto-check results on their phones but not the key.

Warm-up: Weeks 1–5 at Work

  1. broke the ice
  2. figured it out
  3. hit it off
  4. patched things up
  5. came up with
  6. killed time
  7. give up
  8. get along

Part 1: Maya's Year in 6 Texts

Order: C (1) → F (2) → E (3) → B (4) → D (5) → A (6)
So on the student page: A=6, B=4, C=1, D=5, E=3, F=2.
Meanings: landed a job = got a job after trying · on top of things = organized and in control · not pulling his weight = not doing his fair share · burning out = becoming very tired and stressed from too much work · climbing the ladder = moving up to better jobs, step by step

Part 2: Listening

Listen 1, heard: pull his weight, burn out, climb the ladder, on top of things, land a job, figure it out. NOT heard: hit it off, give up.
Listen 2: 1 False, 2 True, 3 True, 4 False, 5 True, 6 False
Listen 3: 1 pulling, 2 burn, 3 climb, 4 on top of, 5 land
Possible answer: softer language for the manager: "I feel the work on our project isn't split evenly." / "Could we look at who is doing what?"

Part 3: Which Expression Fits?

  1. land a job
  2. be on top of things
  3. pull your weight
  4. burn out
  5. climb the ladder
  6. not pull your weight

Part 4: Fill in the Blank

  1. landed
  2. on top of
  3. pull
  4. burn out
  5. climbing / climbed
  6. burned out / burnt out
  7. on top of
  8. landed / has landed / 's landed

Part 6: Real or Weird?

  1. Real
  2. Weird → He got / bought a coffee.
  3. Weird → I'm behind, so I missed three deadlines.
  4. Real
  5. Weird → Not an idiom here; it means nothing.
  6. Real
  7. Weird → I'm so burned out today.
  8. Real
  9. Weird → Burn out is negative: I'm so happy!
  10. Real

Part 7: Present Perfect

  1. has landed (also: 's landed)
  2. has been (also: 's been)
  3. hasn't been pulling (also: has not been pulling, hasn't pulled, has not pulled)
  4. have been working (also: 've been working)
  5. has climbed (also: 's climbed)
  6. burned (also: burnt)

Part 8: Find and Fix

  1. She landed a job at the clinic. (no "on")
  2. I'm so burned out this week. (burnout is a noun; burnt out is also OK)
  3. Everyone needs to pull their weight. (no -s)
  4. He needs to pull his weight on this project. (match the possessive)
  5. My sister has been climbing the ladder for five years. (for + length of time)
  6. I am on top of things at work. (plural)

Part 10: Register Corners (suggested)

  1. Close friend only. Very casual and rude about Kevin; never to your manager.
  2. Manager (best). Polite and professional. Also fine with coworkers.
  3. Job interview or manager. Professional and positive.
  4. Close friend or trusted coworker. Casual complaint.
  5. Anywhere. Neutral. Fine in an interview too.
  6. Close friend (text). Very casual slang. Not in an interview.
  7. Job interview or manager. Professional.
  8. Close friend only, and be careful. Never to your manager.

Exit Ticket

2: I'm burned out. (I'm burnt out is also accepted.) 3: Any polite, no-blame sentence, e.g., "I've been doing extra work on the project. Could we look at how the tasks are split?"

Role-Play Cards (6)

Role-play 1: The Group Project

Situation: Coworkers on a team. The project is due Friday.

A: You have done extra work for three weeks. You're tired. Talk to B about the plan for this week.
B: You know you're behind. You had a reason: your manager asked you to help another department. You want to do better.

Goal: Agree on a fair plan: who does what, and by when. · Use: pull your weight · burn out · be on top of things
Useful: "Can we talk about the project?" · "I feel like..." · "How about if you take...?" · "That sounds fair."
Challenge: Stay friendly. Don't use the words lazy or never.

Role-play 2: Talking to the Manager

Situation: An employee meets their manager.

A: Employee: you've worked 60 hours a week. Explain the problem politely and ask for help.
B: Manager: you didn't know about the problem. The project must finish on time. Find a solution with A.

Goal: Find one or two real solutions. · Use: burn out · pull (their) weight · be on top of things
Useful: "Do you have a minute?" · "I've been working..." · "I'm worried about..." · "What if we...?"
Challenge: Employee: no names, no blame. Manager: ask two follow-up questions.

Role-play 3: Interview Practice

Situation: Two friends. A has a job interview tomorrow.

A: You just landed an interview for a job you really want. You're nervous. Ask B to practice with you.
B: Be the interviewer. Ask: "Tell me about yourself." "How do you stay organized?" "Where do you see yourself in five years?"

Goal: A answers three questions with confidence. · Use: land (an interview) · be on top of things · climb the ladder
Useful: "I've been working as..." · "I use a planner to..." · "In five years, I'd like to..."
Challenge: A: use the present perfect at least twice. B: give one tip at the end.

Role-play 4: Coffee with a Mentor

Situation: A newer employee and an experienced coworker.

A: You want a promotion. Ask B how they moved up so fast.
B: You moved up quickly, but you burned out once. Give honest advice.

Goal: A leaves with three pieces of advice. · Use: climb the ladder · burn out · pull your weight
Useful: "How did you...?" · "What would you do differently?" · "My advice is..."
Challenge: B: tell a short story (real or invented).

Role-play 5: The Good News Call

Situation: A phone call between friends or family members.

A: You just landed a job! (real or invented). Call B and share the news.
B: Be excited! Ask at least four questions: what, where, when, how.

Goal: Celebrate and find out all the details. · Use: land a job · climb the ladder · be on top of things
Useful: "Guess what!" · "No way! Congratulations!" · "When do you start?" · "I'm so happy for you."
Challenge: End the call naturally: "I've got to run, but..."

Role-play 6: Neighbors in the Elevator

Situation: Two neighbors meet in the elevator. (Review: Week 1 small talk)

A: Make small talk. Ask about work.
B: Answer. You have work news (good or bad, real or invented).

Goal: Keep the small talk going for two minutes, then end politely. · Use: any two from today + break the ice / make small talk
Useful: "How's work going?" · "Busy, but good." · "Well, this is my floor. Have a good one!"
Challenge: Ask two follow-up questions each.

Opinion Line Statements (optional, to hold up)

Climbing the ladder is more important than having free time.
It's OK to work 60 hours a week when you're young.
If a coworker isn't pulling their weight, you should tell the manager.
Landing a job is mostly about who you know.
It's easier to stay on top of things with paper than with a phone.
Preventing burnout is the company's job, not the worker's job.

Language Research Report

Verified against American dictionaries. All five expressions are current, common in American English, and fine for A2+/B1 active use.

land a job

Meaning
to get a job, usually after trying hard (a job that many people want)
Pronunciation
LAND a JOB · landed = LAN-did
Grammar
land + a job / an interview / a role / a contract / your dream job
Past: landed · Pronoun: I landed it!
Example
After six months of searching, my cousin landed a job at a bank.
Collocations
land a job / an interview / a role / a client / your dream job / your first job
Register
Neutral to casual. Fine with friends, coworkers, and your boss. In a formal letter, say "I was offered the position."
Learner mistake
NOT "land on a job" or "landed to a job." Land takes the object directly: landed a job.
Produce?
Yes. Use it actively.
Authentic use
"How to land a job in a tough market" (CNBC headline, 2025)

be on top of things

Meaning
to be organized and in control of everything you need to do
Pronunciation
on TOP of things · sounds like "on-TAH-puv things"
Grammar
be / stay / keep + on top of things
be on top of + noun: on top of my email, on top of the schedule
Opposite: I'm behind. / I'm falling behind.
Example
I use a planner to stay on top of things at work.
Collocations
stay on top of things · keep on top of your bills · on top of the schedule / my email / my homework
Register
Neutral. Safe everywhere, even in a job interview: "I use a planner to stay on top of things."
Learner mistake
NOT "on top of thing" or "on the top of things." Always plural: things.
Produce?
Yes. This is one of the 15 core expressions for the Final.
Authentic use
"...keep up with and on top of the technology" (Barron's, 2026)

pull your weight

Meaning
to do your fair share of the work in a group
Pronunciation
PULL your WEIGHT · weight sounds like "wait"
Grammar
The possessive matches the person: I pull my weight / she pulls her weight / he isn't pulling his weight / everyone needs to pull their weight
Often with need to, should, or not.
Example
Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight if we want to finish on time.
Collocations
need to pull your weight · isn't pulling his weight · pull your own weight
Register
Neutral to casual. Be careful: telling someone "You're not pulling your weight" is direct criticism. With a boss, softer is better: "I feel the work isn't split evenly."
Learner mistake
NOT "pull our weights" (no -s) and NOT "He needs to pull your weight." Match the possessive: his weight.
Produce?
Yes, but think about who you are talking to.
Authentic use
Dictionary.com (American Heritage Idioms): to do your fair share

burn out

Meaning
to become very tired and stressed (body and mind) because you worked too hard for too long
Pronunciation
Verb: burn OUT · Noun: BURN-out
Grammar
Verb (no object): I'm burning out. / She burned out after two years.
Adjective: I feel burned out. (AmE) · burnt out is also heard
Noun: burnout (one word) · This job is burning me out.
Example
He burned out after two years of night shifts.
Collocations
feel burned out · on the edge of burnout · burn yourself out · prevent burnout
Register
Neutral. Fine with friends, coworkers, a manager, even a doctor.
Learner mistake
NOT "I'm burnout." Burnout is a noun. Say: I'm burned out. / I'm burning out.
Produce?
Yes. Use it actively.
Authentic use
"Line managers can become completely swamped and burn out." (Fortune, 2026)

climb the ladder

Meaning
to move up to better jobs in a company or career, step by step
Pronunciation
CLIMB the LADder · the b in climb is silent: /klaɪm/
Grammar
climb the (career / corporate) ladder · move up the ladder · a step up the ladder
Present perfect: She has climbed the ladder fast. / He's been climbing the ladder for ten years.
Example
She climbed the corporate ladder from cashier to store manager.
Collocations
climb the corporate ladder · the career ladder · a step up the ladder · move up the ladder
Register
Neutral. Sometimes a little negative: "He only cares about climbing the corporate ladder."
Learner mistake
Don't pronounce the b in climb. And it's not literal: you don't climb on a real ladder.
Produce?
Yes. In the U.S., "corporate ladder" and "career ladder" are the most common forms.
Authentic use
Dictionary.com lists "corporate ladder" as American English

Grammar notes for the teacher

  • burn out is intransitive as a phrasal verb (I'm burning out) but can take an object (This job is burning me out); with a pronoun it splits: burn me out, not burn out me. Merriam-Webster lists both burned out and burnt out; teach burned out as the American model.
  • pull your weight is not separable; the only change is the possessive. Usually in negative or obligation sentences.
  • land = informal meaning "succeed in getting (a job that many people want)" (Oxford Learner's). Takes a direct object.
  • on top of = "in control of, fully informed about" (American Heritage Idioms via Dictionary.com). Common verbs: be / stay / keep.
  • climb the ladder: in American English the fuller forms corporate ladder / career ladder are very common; move up the ladder is a good alternative.
  • Not taught: British things are getting on top of me (= overwhelmed). It means the opposite of I'm on top of things and would confuse A2+ learners.

Listening: why an original dialogue?

Real U.S. podcasts and news clips with all five expressions are long and fast for A2+. Coffee Break is an original 90-second dialogue written for this lesson, recorded with two synthetic American English voices. It includes natural features: fillers (like, honestly), reactions (Uh-oh, Aw, Haha), self-correction (four times? Five!), and a review expression (figure it out). The audio is built into both files and also sent as a separate MP3.

Simpler alternative: read the transcript aloud with a student, slowly, and pause after each expression.

Teacher Notes

Fix in the old Week 7 worksheet (Sasha's packet)

Exercise 5, item 1 marks "She has been burned out since she took the new role" as a grammar error, but the sentence is correct (burned out is an adjective here, like tired). This new set doesn't use that item. If you use the old worksheet, replace it with a real error, e.g., "She has burn out since...".

Personal topics

Work can be sensitive (job loss, immigration-related work status, long hours). Every speaking task in this lesson works with a character, an invented job, or an opinion. The Office Mingle uses character cards only. In role-plays and the Quick Write, students may always say "real or invented".

Differentiation

  • A2+: Toolkit open during speaking, word banks, Useful language lines, first-letter hints, mixed-level pairs.
  • B1: Challenge lines, since/for sentences, rephrase for a different register corner, no-support Round 2 of the Mission, 3+ expressions in the Quick Write.

Assessment connection

  • Final (Week 11): 3–4 minute natural exchange; be on top of things is a core expression. The Conversation Mission rehearses this format (no planning, mixed expressions).
  • Register check: note students who use pull your weight or slang too directly in the manager role-play and give feedback in the wrap-up.
  • Week 10 recycles Weeks 7–8, so keep the mingle and mission cards.

Sharing

  • Student copy: upload week7-student.html to GitHub like previous weeks. It saves answers in each student's browser and auto-checks graded parts. The printable PDF is for students who prefer paper.
  • Teacher copy: keep week7-teacher.html out of the public repo (it contains the answer key).
